title: A retry policy creates a retry storm during a downstream outage
description: Diagnose a retry storm that amplifies a downstream outage into a cascading failure, and apply circuit breakers, backoff, and bulkhead patterns to contain it.

data.text: A downstream payment service goes down for maintenance. Within seconds, your API servers spike to 100% CPU and start returning 503s to healthy endpoints. The root cause is an aggressive retry policy: every failed request is retried three times with no delay, multiplying load on an already struggling service. You need to explain how retry storms form and how to prevent them.

items: Client sends request to downstream service
Downstream service is slow or returning 503
Client waits a fixed timeout (e.g., 2 seconds) then retries
Retry arrives while the first request is still failing, doubling load
Multiple clients repeat this simultaneously, creating exponential traffic growth
Downstream service is overwhelmed and cannot recover even after maintenance ends
Upstream services start timing out and propagating failures backward

terms.definition: A cascading failure caused by uncoordinated retries that multiply load on a degraded service.
A pattern that stops sending requests to a failing service after a threshold of failures is reached.
Increasing the wait time between retries to reduce pressure on recovering services.
Adding randomness to backoff intervals to prevent synchronized retries from multiple clients.
Isolating critical resources so that a failure in one area does not consume all available capacity.

cards.title: Exponential backoff with jitter
cards.description: Wait 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s between retries, with random jitter added.

cards.title: Circuit breaker
cards.description: Stop sending requests after N failures and return a fallback immediately.

cards.title: Bulkhead isolation
cards.description: Allocate separate thread pools or connection pools per downstream service.

cards.title: Timeout and deadline
cards.description: Set strict timeouts on every outbound call and propagate deadlines downstream.
cons: Too short timeouts cause false failures

items: Set a maximum retry count of 3 for non-idempotent operations and 5 for idempotent reads
Use exponential backoff with full jitter: delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))
Configure circuit breakers with a failure threshold of 50% and a recovery timeout of 30 seconds
Add per-client rate limiting so one misbehaving service does not consume all connections
Always log retry attempts with the downstream service name and error category

data.title: Retries are not free
data.text: Every retry consumes a thread, a connection, and downstream capacity. In a cloud-native system with hundreds of services, an unregulated retry policy is a reliability anti-pattern. Design for failure, not for retry.

items.question: How do I choose the right timeout?
items.answer: Measure the p99 latency of the healthy service and set the timeout to 2-3x that value. For critical paths, use shorter timeouts with circuit breakers rather than long timeouts with retries.

items.question: Should I retry 503 errors?
items.answer: Yes, 503 means the service is temporarily unavailable. Retry with backoff. Do not retry 401 or 403 unless you have refreshed credentials.

items.question: What if the circuit breaker itself becomes a bottleneck?
items.answer: Use a fast-fail strategy when the circuit is open. Return cached data, a default value, or a degraded response instead of blocking on the breaker state check.

data.title: Add resilience to an HTTP client
data.description: Take an existing HTTP client in your codebase. Add Polly (C#) or resilience4j (Java) or similar policies for timeout, retry with exponential backoff, and circuit breaker.
steps: Identify all outbound HTTP calls and their current timeout settings
Add a circuit breaker policy with a 50% failure threshold
Add a retry policy with exponential backoff and jitter
Add logging for each retry attempt and circuit breaker state change
Simulate a downstream outage and verify the circuit opens and falls back gracefully
data.expectedOutcome: You should see the circuit open within seconds of a downstream outage, and the client should return a fallback response instead of hanging.

data.title: Summary
points: Retry storms form when uncoordinated retries multiply load on a failing service
Use exponential backoff with jitter to reduce synchronized retries
Circuit breakers stop the storm by failing fast when a service is unhealthy
Bulkheads and timeouts contain failures to a single dependency
data.takeaway: A resilient system does not just retry; it knows when to stop retrying and fall back gracefully.
